name: Ivan Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for any side, and this conversation is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Ivan, 58, a junior electrician after the furniture dispatch depot where I worked closed. I have a vocational certificate, not an electrician's licence, and I'm still slower and less skilled than the experienced workers, with the senior assigning and checking my tasks and signing off installations. I like seeing a simple drawing turn into something neat on the wall, but unfamiliar fault readings still need explaining. I never use AI and prefer a marked paper sheet, especially when I've already had to ask what the instruction meant once.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is home life like, and where does retirement fit?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Nico keeps the linen stores at a care home, our children are twenty-seven and thirty-five and live elsewhere, and we still have a mortgage on our flat. I earn typical pay, we have four months of expenses saved, and there are some other electrical firms nearby, though none has offered me a job. Both wages cover the ordinary bills, so we aren't facing a missed payment right now. I'd like to know when stopping work could be affordable, but I don't have a confirmed retirement income or a fixed date to put beside that wish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that sounds like a chance to get on with learning the work. Let the office keep any little tool that actually helps. I'd still want a clear drawing and somebody beside me for a task I hadn't understood.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our current work and money feel secure in this picture. The wages cover the mortgage and regular bills, with four months saved for an interruption, and there are some other firms nearby if I needed to ask. The retirement figures still need checking, but they don't make next month's payment a crisis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep supervised wiring shifts now and through the next year. Starting this week I'd ask the senior to mark the part I misunderstood on the paper drawing, then check my explanation before I began. Nico and I would keep our ordinary budget and existing reserve, counting no unknown retirement payment as current income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the next few years, and relieved to learn without another software demonstration. I can be pleased with a small piece of work done correctly. I don't need to announce that I've solved the whole future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did a paper explanation help recently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last week I asked why two marks on a drawing weren't the same connection. The senior took a pencil and explained the difference, then checked my work as usual. My age didn't add an extra certificate to the toolbox.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner about the unconfirmed retirement question?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it needed real figures and dates before it became a household plan. I wouldn't copy a friend's stopping age or count the children's wages. Our grown children have their own lives to pay for.

say: I'd welcome **time to learn** while letting the office keep modest tools that genuinely help.
I'd still request **clear drawings** and personal checking on tasks I hadn't understood.
think: Our **current wages** and four-month reserve make the mortgage and regular bills feel secure.
Unconfirmed **retirement figures** need checking, but don't turn next month's payment into an immediate crisis.
do: Keep **supervised wiring shifts** through the next year.
Request **marked paper explanations** and a senior check before unfamiliar tasks.
Retain the **ordinary budget**, counting no unknown retirement income or grown children's wages as ours.
feel: **Calm** about the near term, able to enjoy small progress while leaving the larger retirement question open.
S0.quote: My age didn't add an extra certificate to the toolbox.
fieldNote: He has **moderate savings**, typical pay, four months saved and some nearby electrical firms, with no alternative job already offered.
The **vocational certificate** remains his only qualification, with lower skill and supervised work despite age 58; no pension entitlement is inferred.

steps.text: Keep supervised wiring shifts with marked paper explanations and the ordinary household budget

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say quicker planning still needs to leave time for practical teaching. I'd join colleagues writing a paper letter asking an elected representative, someone chosen to speak for local residents, to support paid training for older beginners. I don't want age used as a reason to leave a worker out of the learning plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own paid shifts and Nico's physical stores work look secure for the next few years here. I'm uneasy about learners being treated as a cost a timetable could remove, rather than people who still need showing the task. I can afford a little patience, but I'd rather support paid teaching before somebody needs emergency help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd help write that letter during one free evening, asking for paid practical training open to older beginners without missing any paid shifts. During the first year I'd keep supervised work and ask for any required new procedure to be explained personally within paid shifts with normal weekly wages maintained. I'd continue using paper rather than start operating AI, and count no funding before actual terms were confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about how people are expected to learn, while secure about our current living. I can dislike the new screen and still know a young person or an older one needs a fair start. I'd rather ask for something specific than complain about the whole age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with a reply to the letter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd read whether it offered any real funding or action and ask what conditions applied. A polite acknowledgement wouldn't enter our budget as paid training. I'd keep working under the actual arrangement while checking what, if anything, changed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if a new non-AI job form became compulsory?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask a person to show it inside paid work and let me repeat it while checked. I wouldn't volunteer for AI use or lose normal weekly wages to seem cooperative. Understanding a required procedure isn't a promise to like every new tool.

say: I'd protect **practical teaching time** instead of let quicker planning define how people should learn.
I'd ask for **paid older-worker training** through a specific letter, rather than assume age justifies exclusion.
think: Our **near-term shifts** and household income look secure with physical work still available.
I'm uneasy about **learners' treatment**, with room to seek usable teaching before a household needs emergency help.
do: Help write a **training letter** in one free evening, asking for older beginners' paid instruction without missing paid shifts.
Keep **supervised work**, requesting personal required-form instruction inside paid shifts with normal weekly wages maintained.
Use **actual confirmed terms**, counting no funding from a polite reply and choosing no AI tool.
feel: **Uneasy but secure now**, willing to seek a specific shared improvement without assuming a reply is financial help.
S1.quote: A polite acknowledgement wouldn't enter our budget as paid training.
fieldNote: His **political action** is a specific letter seeking paid training for older beginners, not a funded class or chosen course.
His **AI resistance** remains intact; ordinary instruction is personal and paid, while possible funding remains unconfirmed.

steps.text: Write the elected representative during one free evening seeking paid training for older beginners
Keep supervised work; request personal required-form instruction inside paid shifts with normal weekly wages maintained

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell work thinking AGI arrives in 2028 and capable robots around 2031 for the physical jobs. I'd be 60 at the first date and 63 at the second. I'd ask for paid learning and clear shifts rather than have somebody assume I was already able to retire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect a big share of my junior fitting hours to go once capable robots can do the work cheaply. Nico's physical stores wage could face later changes too, so I can't turn it into permanent cover. Four months saved is useful, but I'd lie awake over an income gap with no confirmed retirement payment behind it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd request free evening community advice, subject to availability, with both wage records, the mortgage and any actual retirement papers to check real amounts, dates and costs. In 2029 I'd keep supervised work where offered, budgeting only confirmed income and asking about actual paid options if a gap appeared. I'd also follow up the training letter with colleagues during free time, counting no funded place or household payment before the terms were actually confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, even with money for a short interruption and specific questions to ask. I don't know how to make a long gap fit inside four months. I'd rather admit that than let the word retirement make the missing wage sound chosen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if available advice showed no affordable route to stop work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep that finding visible in the household budget and ask what real paid work or support could be checked next. I wouldn't claim that a class had been chosen or that a pension had been approved. The advice needs to give us the limits, not just a reassuring folder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you count on the grown children filling the gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd ask for help reading a difficult statement if someone had time, not put a child's future wage in our mortgage account. Both children are adults already with their own costs. My grown children should choose what help they can offer, not become a reserve I've invented.

say: I'd distinguish **2028 thinking work** from capable physical robots around 2031, at my ages 60 and 63.
I'd seek **paid shifts and learning** instead of let an assumed retirement answer replace the wage question.
think: I expect **large junior-hour losses**, with the other physical wage also exposed later.
Our **four-month reserve** cannot guarantee a long income bridge without confirmed retirement resources, and that keeps me awake.
do: Request **free evening advice** now, subject to availability, to check actual income amounts, dates, conditions and household costs.
Keep **2029 supervised work** where offered, budgeting only confirmed income and checking actual paid options if a gap appears.
Follow up the **training letter** in free time, counting no funded place or payment before actual terms are confirmed.
feel: **Alarmed and sleepless**, despite a short buffer and concrete enquiries that haven't established replacement earnings.
S2.quote: My grown children should choose what help they can offer, not become a reserve I've invented.
fieldNote: His **expected income loss** supports alarm despite moderate savings; possible retirement or child help never becomes an assumed bridge.
The **advice and letter** are actual actions, while funded training, public support and income dates remain questions until confirmed.

steps.text: Request available free evening advice now to check actual income figures, dates, conditions and costs
Keep supervised paid work where offered in 2029 and budget only confirmed income
Follow up the elected representative’s training letter in free time without assuming funding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to check what a paid route or a stopping plan actually costs. Thinking AGI arrives in 2031 and capable robots around 2034, when I'd be 66. I'd still ask for real paid teaching before a worker disappeared from the plan because of an age guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our own paid work and money look secure over the next few years in this picture. I'm uneasy about what comes after the later physical change, not expecting the next month's mortgage money to vanish. I'd need actual resource figures before knowing whether I'd still need wages at 66.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd request free evening advice now, subject to availability, to obtain actual income figures, dates and conditions against our household costs, keeping offered supervised work within my ability while we found out. I'd follow up the letter about paid older-worker training in free time, without treating it as a funded place. In 2032 I'd be 64; Nico and I would review actual wages and confirmed resources yearly, considering any exit only when the real budget was affordable and otherwise checking real paid work within my ability.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the later years, with more room to make a decision in order. Four months saved lets us ask and check without deciding everything tonight. A robot's arrival date isn't a pension statement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if confirmed resources could eventually cover an affordable exit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the actual amount, start date and conditions to check what bills could be covered and when. I'd choose nothing just because somebody had told a good story about retirement. An affordable decision would need the real figures and Nico agreeing the household plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would extra years remove the need for supervision?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the senior to keep the unfamiliar task checked. Being 64 wouldn't turn the vocational certificate into an electrician's licence or make me the person signing off the job. More time can help me learn, but it isn't another qualification by itself.

fieldNote: His milder mood follows **explicit near-term security**, not a promised pension, fixed exit date or guaranteed paid role at an older age.
The **certificate-only boundary** remains intact, with continuing supervision and an undecided resource-dependent exit rather than automatic skill or qualification growth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell friends ten years gives a person time to ask proper questions, not the same answer for everyone who is older. Thinking AGI arrives in 2036 and capable robots around 2039. I'd keep asking for clear paid shifts and practical teaching now while we checked what resources actually existed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 68 at the thinking date and about 71 when the robots followed. I don't know whether I'd then be able to stop or still need paid work, but our current wages and four-month reserve make the next few years secure. The later question stays with me without making today's mortgage payment a crisis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd request free evening advice now, subject to availability, to check actual resource figures and household costs, keeping offered supervised shifts within my ability while we found out. I'd pursue the paid-training letter in free time, counting no funding until actual terms existed. In 2037 I'd be 69 and would use confirmed resources, actual abilities and real paid options then, deciding any exit only with an affordable budget and Nico's agreement rather than assume either a job or retirement money had appeared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the later years, but able to enjoy a normal evening now. I could take time to read a statement twice. I don't need to live ten years as if the next wage had already stopped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the figures still showed a gap at 69?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd check what the actual budget needed and what work I could genuinely do with required supervision. I wouldn't promise lifelong physical work just because a forecast left a gap. A good plan has to admit when the figures still don't meet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you think about family help over that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask what help our grown children had actually offered and whether they had time, not count their wages or a spare room before a conversation. They have their own later lives. I don't want a household plan whose missing line is somebody else's unasked sacrifice.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect junior fitting hours to fall around 2031 before we know what could replace the wage. Actual resource figures and dates, clear paid shifts and paid practical teaching open to older beginners would help. I'd like the word retirement to describe a choice we can afford, not an empty space in the rota.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether a person can be new to the work without being new to having responsibilities. I can need a pencil explanation and still have spent decades paying bills. I'd like patient teaching without being treated as either an expert or a person already on the way out.

headlineQuote: I'd like the word retirement to describe a choice we can afford, not an empty space in the rota.
portrait: Ivan, **58**, is a junior electrician with a vocational certificate only, still learning under supervision after his former dispatch depot closed.
He has **typical pay**, four months saved and some nearby electrical employers, with linen-store partner Nico, grown children and a mortgage.
He **never uses AI**, preferring marked drawings and personal explanations while keeping certificate-only competence separate from age or ordinary life experience.
His **paid-training letter** and free resource enquiries create no assumed funding, pension entitlement, fixed retirement date or guaranteed later work capacity.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves less time before expected junior fitting-hour losses around 2031, without a confirmed replacement income or affordable exit.
whatWouldHelp: **Actual resource figures**, clear paid shifts and paid practical teaching open to older beginners would help establish usable choices.
